# Policy Learning: History, Roots, and Branches

## Introduction 

Before turning to information processing as a micro-foundational hinge for learning, it is useful to briefly explore the genealogy and landscape of the policy learning literature. The contemporary conceptual landscape did not emerge as an abstract exercise in classification. Rather, it crystallized through successive attempts to make sense of how policy actors confront uncertainty, novel policy problems, the contestation that surrounds them, and how they mobilize knowledge under institutional constraints. A brief reconstruction of these roots helps explain both why policy learning became such an expansive field of study and why, as the field matured, it generated multiple branches that sometimes converge and sometimes compete. This historical sketch, therefore, provides the groundwork for the syntheses and distinctions that follow.

The contemporary foundations of learning in public policy and administration were laid decades ago by trailblazers such as @deweyPublicItsProblems1946, @deutschNervesGovernmentModels1963, @lasswellEmergingConceptionPolicy1970, @lasswellPolicyOrientation1951, among others. This early intellectual stream was underpinned by an understanding of administration and policymaking as problem-oriented practices, continuously pressed to respond to novel, unfolding societal challenges [@kaufmanAdministrativeDecentralizationPolitical1969]. It was also animated by a view of policymaking as a process of collective problem-solving and  "puzzling", rather than merely a sequence of decisions imposed through power [@hecloModernSocialPolitics1974]. In this spirit, early learning scholarship sought to strengthen the link between knowledge and action by bringing together publics, stakeholders, and scientific communities to address societal problems. Its central tenet was a pragmatist orientation toward discovering what works, avoiding what does not, and building forms of stakeholder collaboration capable of sustaining informed collective action. In doing so, learning offered a supplementary, and often less visible, explanatory dimension to policy analysis [@hallPolicyParadigmsSocial1993; @hecloModernSocialPolitics1974; @zakiMeasuringPolicyLearning2024]. 

This pragmatic, solution-oriented foundation also helps explain the subsequent expansion of policy learning research and practice. Accelerating technological and industrial change, more tightly connected ecologies, and rising complexity generated policy problems that were increasingly difficult to define, depoliticize, or settle, and that came to be described through an expanding vocabulary of "wickedness," "turbulence," and "crises" [@headWickedProblemsImplications2015; @rittelDilemmasGeneralTheory1973; @boinHidingPlainSight2020; @zakiPracticingPolicyLearning2024]. As policy problems became more contested and less tractable, inclusive, deliberate, and cumulative learning processes, whether at individual or collective levels, were increasingly positioned as central to developing workable responses.

In parallel, policy learning emerged as a practice, as actors increasingly engaged in more systematic efforts to learn over time, across jurisdictions, and across sectors. From the 1970s onward, scholarship documented this growth across domains ranging from environmental and climate governance to welfare, economic policy, and public health, as well as crisis governance and emergency politics [@crowPolicyLearningChange2023; @dunlopIronyEpistemicLearning2017; @hecloModernSocialPolitics1974; @shiSocialPolicyLearning2012; @gerlakLearningOurWay2018; @leeWhoTeachesWho2012; @rietigLeveragingPowerLearning2019; @kamkhajiCrisisLearningPolicy2017; @taylorExerciseDisasterDoes2022; @treinLearningHeuristicsIssue2022]. Institutional arrangements were also developed to scaffold learning, whether through benchmarking, mutual adjustment, cross-jurisdictional comparison, and cross-sectoral exchange, including prominent instruments in the European Union such as the Open Method of Coordination and the European Semester, as well as internal coordination practices [@borrasOpenMethodCoOrdination2004; @kerberPolicyLearningEurope2007]. Likewise, transnational and thematic networks have pursued learning-oriented objectives by enabling shared metrics, peer exchange, and diffusion of practices [@candelPatternsCoordinationEuropean2023; @leeWhoTeachesWho2012].

Interest in policy learning did not only manifest at the apex of governance architectures. Beyond the European Union and transnational policy networks, learning occurs at sub-national levels, including provinces, cities, and local communities, where proximity to implementation, service delivery, and community problem-solving often makes learning both more immediate and more consequential [@ansellHowLearningAggregates2017; @busettiPolicyLearningCrises2023; @zakiHowDoesPolicy2023; @marshallStreetlevelBureaucratsPolicy2019]. So, one can comfortably say that the expanding practice of learning has, in turn, fueled theoretical development, contributing to what @dunlopLearningPublicPolicy2018 describe as "the family tree of policy learning," boasting roots that sprouted into multiple branches. What began at the roots as collective puzzlement oriented toward workable solutions, reflections on knowledge utilization [@weissResearchPolicyMakingLimited1986], public engagement in problem-solving [@deweyPublicItsProblems1946; @lasswellEmergingConceptionPolicy1970], negotiated adjustments [@lindblomScienceMuddling1959], and boundedly rational information processing within governmental and societal networks [@simonAdministrativeBehaviorStudy1997], has since grown into a set of interrelated branches. These include subfields centered around ideas and ideational change [@etteltPolicyLearningAbroad2012], the mobility of policies through transfer, diffusion, and convergence [@dolowitzLearningAbroadRole2000], information processing and attention dynamics [@nowlinPolicyLearningInformation2021; @zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022], evidence use and evaluative learning [@sandersonIntelligentPolicyMaking2009], and typological approaches that differentiate learning according to actor objectives and contextual conditions [@biegelbauerHowDifferentForms2016; @dunlopSystematisingPolicyLearning2013]. Following the same metaphor, these branches also bear different analytical "fruits", ranging from design-oriented and governance approaches that treat learning as something that can be deliberately shaped [@dunlopLearningBathTubMicro2017; @heikkilaBuildingConceptualApproach2013; @zakiHelloDarknessMy2024], to causal accounts linking learning to belief and policy change [@dunlopLearningBathTubMicro2017; @sabatierPolicyChangeLearning1993]    


Taken together, this history helps explain why policy learning grew into a family tree, with multiple branches that share ancestry yet differ in their conceptual commitments and empirical objects of concern. This breadth has been productive, but it has also created a familiar trade-off between inclusiveness and precision. As learning spans theories and domains, it becomes easier to invoke it as an umbrella term than to specify exactly what varies, how learning is instantiated, and how it can be identified across studies. This is the terrain of conceptual stretching and "overlapping contours" that motivates repeated calls for synthesis and systematization [@borrasPolicyLearningOrganizational2011; @dunlopSystematisingPolicyLearning2013; @gerlakLearningOurWay2018; @levyLearningForeignPolicy1994; @zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022]. The next section responds by mapping the field in a way that retains its pluralism while clarifying its core orientations, units, and analytical descriptors, thereby setting up a more organized foundation for the information-processing focus developed later in this element.


## Policy Learning: A Synthesis of Key Conceptual, Analytical, and Theoretical Approaches

### Key Conceptual Approaches 


The increasing recognition of policy learning as a key lens for policy analysis has generated a flurry of research. While this output has enriched the field, it has also produced a sprawling vocabulary of partially overlapping concepts and descriptors that are not always clearly mapped or systematically arranged. The multilevel and often implicit nature of learning, combined with its normative appeal, further compounds this problem by making learning conceptually slippery and empirically hard to pin down. The result is a hegemonic yet overextended concept, vulnerable to conceptual stretching, definitional ambiguity, and difficulties in systematizing and comparing findings across studies. In this sense, work on policy learning risks resembling the sort of "minefield" of conceptual stretching long associated with over-scoped concepts [@levyLearningForeignPolicy1994]. Recent reviews echo this diagnosis, describing a "conceptual jungle" in which overlapping approaches proliferate and consensus over even a small set of usable definitions remains elusive [@borrasPolicyLearningOrganizational2011; @gerlakLearningOurWay2018]. This state of affairs has stimulated recurrent calls for theoretical and conceptual syntheses on which further field development can be anchored [@dunlopLessonsPolicyLearning2018; @goyalLessonsLearnedNot2018; @zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022]. Accordingly, and before delving into the information-processing dimension of policy learning, it is useful to first lay out the field’s key conceptual and theoretical approaches. The objective is twofold: first, to provide a succinct synthesis of an otherwise sprawling literature; and second, to establish a robust foundation for mapping the dynamics of policy learning and the role of information processing within it.


We begin by discussing what policy learning is. Sustained interest in learning has generated a diversity approaches of defining and operationalizing it, often distinguished by their underlying ontological orientations and epistemic commitments [@dunlopLearningBathTubMicro2017; @zakiMeasuringPolicyLearning2024]. Across this spectrum, scholars have mobilized perspectives, ranging from more mechanistic and positivist accounts to interpretivist, social-constructivist, and discursive-institutionalist [@grinTheoriesPolicyLearning2007; @oliverLearningChange20thCentury2004]. In constructivist–interpretivist work, learning is foregrounded as an inherently social process through which actors negotiate problem definitions and meanings, communicate, interpret, and assess solution claims [@grinImplementationCommunicativeAction1996]. By contrast, other strands, most prominently those rooted in the Advocacy Coalition Framework (ACF), emphasize how actors process new information through relatively coherent pre-existing belief systems, with learning unfolding as belief updating under cognitive and political constraints [@sabatierPolicyChangeLearning1993; @dudleySymposiumTheoriesPolicy2000]. In ontological-epistemological terms, this positions learning closer to a presuppositionist, neo-positivist view in which beliefs structure information processing and observable belief change becomes a primary empirical trace of learning. 


The ontological and epistemological diversity spills over into the field’s conceptual landscape, where policy learning is associated with a wide range of definitions and partially overlapping conceptual approaches. Literature reviews identify more than thirty distinct definitions of learning in the public policy literature [@zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022]. Among the most prominent is the ACF's formulation, which treats learning as enduring changes in thought, beliefs, or behavioral intentions regarding policy problems [@sabatierPolicyChangeLearning1993]. Other influential definitions conceptualize learning more instrumentally as deliberate adjustment of policy goals and techniques in response to experience and new information [@hallPolicyParadigmsSocial1993]. 

Beyond these, other work sees policy learning as an umbrella that captures the broader mobility of ideas and practices, encompassing phenomena such as lesson drawing, emulation, transfer, and diffusion across time and space [@giestOvercomingFailureSilicon2017]. Other conceptualizations emphasize learning as an increase or update in knowledge about policy problems [@corbettSingularMemoryInstitutional2018], as reflective reasoning about policy using acquired knowledge and information [@newmanBritishColumbiasFast2017], or as processes of acquisition, translation, and dissemination of information among actors with heterogeneous knowledge bases [@heikkilaBuildingConceptualApproach2013]. Finally, some approaches treat learning as a decision-making paradigm in which policymaking is structured by knowledge, past experience, and anticipations of future consequences [@karlsenMovingContextBackground2017]. Taken together, these conceptualizations can be organized into four broad perspectives on policy learning, namely process-oriented, paradigmatic, outcome-oriented, and idea-oriented. @tbl-learn-concept summarizes these perspectives, their core emphases, and representative contributions.


| **Perspective** | **Conceptualization** |
| :---: | ----- |
| **Process-oriented: Focused on how learning takes place** | The acquisition, translation, and dissemination of information among actors with diverse knowledge bases [@heikkilaBuildingConceptualApproach2013]. The transmission of policy knowledge between political actors [@legrandOverseasHerePolicy2012]. Deliberate and critical reflection on prior knowledge [@rietigDoesLearningMatter2018]. |
| **Paradigmatic: Learning as a decisional approach or a policymaking style** | An approach to policymaking where policy decisions are made based on knowledge and past experiences and future expectations [@karlsenMovingContextBackground2017]. Learning as a deliberate attempt to adjust the goals or techniques of policy in response to experience and new information [@hallPolicyParadigmsSocial1993]. |
| **Outcome-oriented: Focused on the products of learning such as cognitive updates and changes in policy positions** | Enduring changes in thoughts, beliefs, or behavioral intentions regarding policy problems [@sabatierPolicyChangeLearning1993]. The general increase in knowledge about policies [@corbettSingularMemoryInstitutional2018]. |
| **Idea-oriented: Learning as the mobility of ideas and policies across time and space** | A process whereby knowledge about policy in one jurisdiction is acquired and utilized in decisions regarding the development of policies in another [@newmanBritishColumbiasFast2017]. Drawing lessons from experiences, and using knowledge to inform policy action [@mottaPolicyDiffusionDirectionality2018]. |

: A Non-Exhaustive Synthesis of Conceptual Approaches to Policy Learning {#tbl-learn-concept}


With a multitude of definitions existing, many of which have been reviewed above, we now circle back to what learning is at a fundamental level. Here, one way of to navigate and systematize this proliferation of definitions in the policy learning literature is to distinguish between a concept’s background meaning and its more systematized variants, thereby clarifying what the concept is fundamentally about before tracing how it is specified across different research traditions  [see @adcockMeasurementValidityShared2001]. At this foundational level, policy learning can be understood as an iterative, problem-oriented process in which policy actors embedded in sensemaking and institutional structures seek and process information about policy issues with the aim of updating their understandings of how these issues can be addressed within an evolving context [@zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022]. Such updating can yield different products, including cognitive outcomes, such as developing or revising beliefs and understandings of policy problems and plausible solutions, and, in some cases, behavioral outcomes, such as deploying political strategies and adjusting or changing policies in response to those updated understandings [@heikkilaBuildingConceptualApproach2013].

Adopting this view, which foregrounds the fundamental role of information in the learning process, and making explicit its constitutive analytical dimensions (information and knowledge, actors, learning structures, policy problems, and context), provides a common baseline for identifying learning across conceptually diverse strands. For instance, policy transfer and lesson drawing can be approached as a learning process organized around the movement and use of policy-relevant information across time and/or space, where actors draw on external experiences or jurisdictions to inform domestic choices [e.g., @dolowitzLearningAbroadRole2000; @roseWhatLessonDrawing1991; @voldenFormalModelLearning2008]. An information-processing lens then helps structure analysis by specifying what information is mobilized, from which sources, by whom, and through which cognitive and governance structures it is selected, interpreted, translated, and institutionalized.

With these conceptual foundations and streams in place, we now turn to key theoretical perspectives that further specify learning in analytical terms, focusing on descriptors such as forms, mechanisms, modes, and types of learning.


### Key Analytical Approaches: Learning as Levels of Analysis

As discussed, several approaches have emerged to describe policy learning processes and capture a diverse set of learning phenomena. The concept of learning, therefore, affords multiple analytical vantage points on the policy process, not least because learning can be theorized as operating at different levels of analysis and through different pathways. In this sense, policy learning is positioned to explain related behavior at the micro level of individuals, the meso level of groups, organizations, and subsystems, and the macro level of broader institutional and societal dynamics, while also allowing for multidimensional and non-linear patterns in which learning unfolds across levels and loops back on itself. @tbl-learn-levels summarizes these levels and dynamics, providing brief descriptions and illustrative examples of micro-, meso-, and macro-level learning, as well as multidimensional and non-linear learning trajectories.


| **Levels of Analysis** | **Examples** |
| ----- | ----- |
| **Micro-level: Focus on individuals and cognitive foundations** | Learning as a cognitive micro foundational process [@beachPresentRoleAnalogical2021], behavioral perspectives moderating learning [@zitoEuropeanAgenciesAgents2009], the role of individual beliefs and information flows in learning [@moysonCognitionPolicyChange2017; @nowlinPolicyLearningInformation2021; @pattisonFactorsShapingPolicy2018], biases and heuristics [@heikkilaDiagnosingIndividualBarriers2024; @malkamakiAcousticsPolicyLearning2021; @wagnerCanPolicyForums2020]. |
| **Meso-level: Focus on organizational units, collectives, and networks** | Learning as interactions with information and beliefs within and across advocacy coalitions [@sabatierPolicyChangeLearning1993; @weibleExpertBasedInformationPolicy2008], learning as interaction within and with expert communities [@haasIntroductionEpistemicCommunities1992], learning within networks [@howlettPolicyLearningPolicy2017], learning within organizations [@borrasPolicyLearningOrganizational2011; @zakiUnderstandingPoliticalLearning2024; @zitoEuropeanAgenciesAgents2009], learning by public organizations focused on public problem solving [@zakiPolicyLearningPolicy2026]. |
| **Macro-level: Focus on systems** | Learning and deliberation in transnational policy issues and crises [@dunlopCantGetNo2020], collective puzzlement and the role of ideas and paradigms [@hallPolicyParadigmsSocial1993; @hecloModernSocialPolitics1974], learning as an inter-system transfer and diffusion of ideas [@dolowitzLearningAbroadRole2000; @marshPolicyDiffusionPolicy2009], learning and systemic convergence towards certain policy ideas [@bennettWhatPolicyConvergence1991]. |
| **Multidimensional and non-linear learning: Focus on cross-level interactions** | Learning as a multidimensional and interactive process between micro, macro, and meso levels [@dunlopLearningBathTubMicro2017], the interaction of learning types over time, learning type shifts and interactions over time [@biegelbauerHowDifferentForms2016; @zakiPolicyLearningEvidence2024]. |

: Learning as Levels of Analysis {#tbl-learn-levels}

With the key analytical perspectives in the policy learning literature established, we next turn our attention to the various theoretical descriptors of policy learning, i.e., the various theoretical perspectives by which learning processes can be described.

### Key Theoretical Perspectives: Disentangling Theoretical Descriptors of Learning

Once learning is located across levels of analysis, the next challenge becomes analytic vocabulary. Against a backdrop of ontological–epistemological diversity and the resulting conceptual pluralism, the field has accumulated a wide repertoire of learning descriptors that often appear interchangeable in practice, even when they point to different aspects of the learning process. Many of these descriptors have emerged inductively from empirical analyses and are frequently bundled under the catch-all label "types of learning," yet often lack the definitional precision and dimensional grounding needed for reliable identification and differentiation [@gerlakLearningOurWay2018; @zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022]. In what follows, we therefore disentangle the most common descriptor families by clarifying the specific question that each of these descriptors answers. This is not a taxonomic exercise for its own sake. It is a prerequisite for identifying learning reliably and linking claims about learning to the mechanisms that plausibly generate observable outcomes. Accordingly, we distinguish between **forms**, **modes**, **mechanisms**, **types**, and **outcomes** of learning, as summarized in @tbl-learn-descript, pivoting on the understanding of policy learning as a process fundamentally concerned with the circulation and consumption of policy-relevant information and knowledge by policy actors.


| **Forms of Learning** | **Modes of Learning** | **Mechanisms of Learning** | **Types of Learning** | **Outcomes of learning** |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | -------- | 
| Lesson drawing Policy Transfer and emulation | Epistemic Hierarchical Reflexive  Bargaining-oriented  | Contingent  Inferential  | Instrumental  Social Managerial Political Single loop Double loop Triple loop Organizational Governance Narrative | Cognitive: updates in knowledge, understandings, beliefs/paradigms, and problem definitions. Behavioral: changes in advocacy/coalition strategies and in policy or organizational practice, including policy stability/lock-in or policy change (e.g., instrument calibration, instrument replacement, or goal/paradigm change)


: A Non-Exhaustive Account of Theoretical Descriptors of Learning {#tbl-learn-descript}

**Forms of learning**. If learning can be broadly understood as a process involving policy actors seeking and processing information and knowledge about policy problems, then forms of learning denote the relatively stable, patterned routes and formats through which policy actors seek, access, and acquire information and knowledge, prior to interpretation and use. The canonical examples sit in the family of trans-jurisdictional knowledge mobility, including _policy transfer_ as the broad umbrella through which information about policies, administrative arrangements, and institutions is sourced in one context and used in another [@dolowitzWhoLearnsWhat1996], alongside diffusion as a more patterned interdependence-driven route of cue sourcing across jurisdictions [@shipanMechanismsPolicyDiffusion2008; @shipanPolicyDiffusionSeven2012], and _convergence-producing pathways_ such as harmonization or emulation that structure how knowledge flows in ways that can facilitate similarity in policy. Within the same forms category, _lesson drawing_ is better treated as a comparatively more deliberate, problem-oriented scan across time and space for solutions to evaluate or avoid [@roseWhatLessonDrawing1991], as are institutionalized formats such as _benchmarking_ and _peer learning_ organized through indicators, _peer review_, and _performance comparison_.

**Modes of learning**. Once information and knowledge are "in," learning still varies systematically in how it is enacted through recurring interactional environments. Modes of learning capture these patterned teacher–learner relations and the participation structures through which knowledge is encountered, negotiated, and validated. These modes of learning, parsimoniously captured by a framework of learning genera developed by @dunlopSystematisingPolicyLearning2013, involves four distinct modes: Reflexive, Hierarchical, Bargaining-oriented, and Epistemic. _Reflexive_ learning unfolds through deliberative exchange among heterogeneous stakeholders aimed at widening debate and revising shared understandings, typically under low tractability and low agreement on who counts as an authoritative problem-solver. _Hierarchical_ learning is organized around authority and compliance, where learning is steered through asymmetric power relations, rules, and institutional constraints that channel what can be learned and toward which objectives. _Bargaining-oriented_ learning is often a spillover of negotiation and contestation in which information serves as a strategic resource to broker agreement through concessions, often without deep preference revision. _Epistemic_ learning is structured by knowledge asymmetries between certified experts and non-expert learners, with expert authority grounded in socially recognized standards and used to reduce ambiguity and delineate feasible options.

**Mechanisms of learning**. If modes describe the setting in which learning is instantiated, mechanisms of learning specify the within-setting causal processing through which informational inputs are converted into cognitive and behavioral adjustment. Following @kamkhajiCrisisLearningPolicy2017,  a useful distinction separates _inferential_ and _contingent_ mechanisms. Inferential learning proceeds through deliberate reasoning about experience and cause–and-effect relations, with belief updating occurring before (or alongside) behavioral change; under acute time pressure, this mechanism often reappears ex post, when feedback allows actors to stabilize interpretations and justify what has been done. Contingent learning, by contrast, is a fast associative pathway triggered by surprise, where salient cue–outcome pairings generate rapid behavioral shifts without prior deliberation, effectively fusing cognition and action under “change-or-die” conditions; inferential processing may then return to consolidate, rationalize, or lock in the emergent trajectory.


**Types of learning**. Against this backdrop, types of learning denote the objects of learning, meaning what actors learn about, or the substantive target domain in which they acquire knowledge, update understandings, or adjust beliefs and practices. The classics remain analytically useful precisely because they specify distinct objects. _Instrumental_ learning concerns what actors come to know about policy instruments, including technical viability, effectiveness, efficiency, and calibration [@mayPolicyLearningFailure1992]. _Social_ learning concerns what actors come to know about the social construction of policy issues and the interpretation of paradigms that organize legitimate goals and solutions [@bennettLessonsLearningReconciling1992; @hallPolicyParadigmsSocial1993] (Hall, 1993). _Managerial_ learning centers on implementation arrangements and administrative routines [@biegelbauerHowDifferentForms2016], while _political_ learning focuses on what actors learn about political feasibility, coalition dynamics, and advocacy strategy [@zakiUnderstandingPoliticalLearning2024]. The loop-learning tradition can be read in the same object-centered way: _single-loop_ learning targets the operational performance of existing routines (including instrument settings and day-to-day adjustments); _double-loop_ learning targets how policy is done (instrument choice, settings, and the working assumptions linking instruments to goals); and _triple-loop_ learning targets what policy is for and why (goals, paradigms, values, and worldviews that structure problem definitions and legitimate solutions). Beyond these, additional types sharpen the object of learning in other domains. For example, _Organizational_ learning concerns organizational routines, procedures, and viability [@schoutOrganizationalLearningEUs2010]. On the other hand, _Organizational policy learning_ focuses on what organizations learn about mobilizing resources and capacities to shape policymaking and governance, thereby linking learning to shifts in organizational capabilities and assessments of what is feasible in practice [@zakiPolicyLearningPolicy2026]. _Governance_ learning concerns what actors learn about governance designs and arrangements, including the rules, procedures, and participation architectures through which collective action is organized [@challiesGovernanceChangeGovernance2017]. _Narrative_ learning concerns what actors learn about the policy narrative itself, including updates to the narrative configuration through which problems and solutions are represented (setting, characters, plot, and moral), as well as the beliefs and strategies embedded in that configuration [@shanahanNarrativePolicyFramework2018].

**Outcomes of learning**. With forms, modes, mechanisms, and types specified, the final step is to clarify what learning produces. Fundamentally, policy learning yields two broad sets of outcomes: cognitive and behavioral. Cognitive products concern changes in understandings and beliefs, whether confirmatory or disconfirmatory, while behavioral products concern changes in action and practice, including policy change or policy stability, as well as shifts in political advocacy strategies and tactics [@heikkilaBuildingConceptualApproach2013; @zakiUnderstandingPoliticalLearning2024]. In these terms, a learning outcome can be understood as any change in a policy process, policy, institution, or actor behavior that can be plausibly linked to a learning process, even if empirically demonstrating causal influence remains difficult [@zakiMeasuringPolicyLearning2024]. Cognitively, learning may update policy beliefs (the lenses through which actors interpret problems and instrument effects, including fundamental values and policy-relevant ideas) without necessarily shifting policy preferences (actors’ goals and evaluative stances in a given context). Learning is therefore "consistent" when preferences are brought into alignment with updated beliefs, which helps explain why observable belief change does not always translate into immediate behavioral change [@plumerWhenDoesPolicy2024]. Behaviorally, the magnitude of change associated with learning is often captured through @hallPolicyParadigmsSocial1993 three "orders" of change: first-order change calibrates existing instrument settings while leaving instruments and overarching goals intact; second-order change alters the instruments (and their settings) while keeping the hierarchy of goals largely stable; and third-order change denotes a paradigm shift involving simultaneous change in settings, instruments, and goals, typically accompanied by a redefinition of policy discourse [@hallPolicyParadigmsSocial1993]. Finally, learning should not be equated with change by default: it can also contribute to stability and confirmation by reinforcing policy-related beliefs and sustaining existing policy choices, as highlighted in advocacy coalition research and institutionalist accounts [@weibleAdvocacyCoalitionsBeliefs2022; @migoneParadigmaticStabilityIdeational2024].


## Conclusion 

The review of the vibrant policy learning literature above shows a landscape sprawling with a wide range of ontologies and conceptual and theoretical approaches that continue to grow through empirical analyses across diverse policy domains. While this literature continues to provide insights into policy processes and outcomes, the persistent issue of how learning occurs at the micro-foundational level and aggregates across the micro, meso, and macro levels, from individuals to collectives, remains scarcely theorized and challenging to address [@dunlopLearningBathTubMicro2017; @jonesBehavioralRationalityFoundation2017].

This chapter illustrates why policy learning is simultaneously a generative research program and a conceptually crowded field, largely because it spans levels and traditions, and is described through multiple descriptor families that do not always align cleanly. Yet this mapping also clarifies what remains undertheorized in much learning scholarship, namely the micro-foundational logic through which learning is produced rather than merely inferred from outcomes. If learning is fundamentally about updating beliefs and understandings in relation to policy problems, then explanation ultimately requires a defensible account of how policy-relevant information is encountered, selected, weighted, and reconciled with priors under cognitive and institutional constraints. Chapter 3 takes up this hinge point directly by developing a model of learning through information processing, thereby connecting the field’s conceptual richness to clearer causal mechanisms that can travel across micro and meso levels and support more cumulative inference.
